Theory of Computation: Finite Automata and Regular Languages A Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) is formally defined as a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q_0, F), where Q is a finite set of states, Sigma is a finite alphabet of input symbols, delta is the transition function mapping Q x Sigma to Q, q_0 in Q is the initial start state, and F subset of Q is the set of accept (or final) states. DFAs recognize the class of regular languages. A Non-Deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) differs in its transition function, which maps Q x (Sigma union {epsilon}) to the power set 2^Q, allowing state transitions on empty strings (epsilon transitions) or multiple possible subsequent states for a single symbol. Despite this flexibility, the subset construction algorithm proves that NFAs and DFAs have equivalent computational power: any NFA with n states can be converted to an equivalent DFA with at most 2^n states.

Virtual Memory and Page Replacement Algorithms Virtual memory decouples the user's logical memory from physical memory, allowing execution of processes whose address spaces exceed available physical RAM. Memory is organized into fixed-size blocks called pages (in logical memory) and frames (in physical memory). When a process attempts to access a page not currently residing in physical RAM, the memory management unit (MMU) generates a page fault hardware interrupt. When a page fault occurs and all memory frames are occupied, a page replacement algorithm must select a victim frame to swap out: - FIFO (First-In, First-Out): Replaces the oldest page loaded in memory. Can suffer from Belady's Anomaly, where increasing the number of page frames results in an increased number of page faults. - Optimal (OPT / Belady's Min): Replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Provides the lowest page fault rate but is impossible to implement in practice because future references cannot be known. - Least Recently Used (LRU): Replaces the page that has not been used for the longest period in the past. Approximates the optimal algorithm by using past temporal locality.

Turing Machines and the Halting Problem A Turing Machine (TM) is a formal model of computation introduced by Alan Turing in 1936. It consists of an infinite memory tape divided into cells and a read/write tape head. The transition function delta maps Q x Gamma to Q x Gamma x {L, R}, where Gamma is the tape alphabet. The Church-Turing thesis states that any algorithm or effectively calculable function can be simulated by a Turing machine. The Halting Problem asks whether a given Turing machine M will halt on a specific input string w. Turing proved that the language A_TM = {<M, w> | M is a Turing Machine and M halts on input w} is undecidable using a diagonal argument. If a decider H for the halting problem existed, one could construct an adversarial machine D that reverses H's decision on its own description, yielding an insurmountable logical contradiction (D halts if and only if D does not halt).

OSI Reference Model vs TCP/IP Protocol Stack The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model, developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), is a conceptual framework with seven distinct architectural layers: 1. Physical Layer: Transmission and reception of raw unstructured bit streams over physical media. 2. Data Link Layer: Node-to-node frame transfer, media access control (MAC), and error detection (CRC). 3. Network Layer: Multi-hop routing, packet forwarding, and logical addressing (IPv4, IPv6). 4. Transport Layer: End-to-end process-to-process communication, multiplexing (TCP, UDP). 5. Session Layer: Dialog control, token management, and synchronization checkpoints. 6. Presentation Layer: Syntax translation, character encoding, data compression, and encryption/SSL. 7. Application Layer: High-level network application services (HTTP, DNS, SMTP, FTP). Operating Systems: Process Synchronization and Deadlocks In multiprogramming environments, concurrent access to shared data can lead to data inconsistency. A race condition arises when several processes access and manipulate the same data concurrently and the outcome depends on the particular order in which access takes place. The critical-section problem requires three structural conditions to be satisfied: 1. Mutual Exclusion: If process P_i is executing in its critical section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical sections. 2. Progress: If no process is executing in its critical section and there exist some processes that wish to enter their critical section, then only those processes not executing in their remainder sections can participate in deciding which will enter next. 3.
